Stolid

STOL-id · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Stolid is calm, dependable, and showing little emotion.

The stolid old dog barely lifted its head when the fireworks began.

Worked Example

The stolid negotiator kept the exact same expression whether the offer was generous or insulting.

Nothing shook the negotiator's outward calm, no matter how the situation changed -- that steady, unemotional composure is exactly stolid.

How Stolid Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

impassive

impassive: showing no emotion or feeling

unflappable

unflappable: not easily upset or excited

Antonyms

excitable

excitable: quick to become emotional or agitated

How Strong Is It? — reserved → wooden → stolid

reserved vs. stolid

reserved vs. stolid: Being reserved just means not talkative or expressive; being stolid means staying calm and unemotional even under real pressure.

wooden vs. stolid

wooden vs. stolid: A stolid person is calm but still natural; a wooden one seems unnaturally stiff and lifeless.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Stolid comes directly from Latin stolidus, 'dull, slow, and unmoved,' with no further breakdown -- it's one solid piece rather than a root plus a suffix.

Use the root in a new word: stolid

Use the root in a new word: stolid: Stolidus is one of Latin's more isolated roots; it never spread into a wider modern-English word family beyond stolid itself.

Root Check

Word Choice

Stolid is usually a compliment describing someone reliably calm under pressure. You already met its closest cousin, impassive, in the immediately preceding unit -- impassive emphasizes a controlled FACIAL expression in one moment, while stolid describes an overall calm, dependable TEMPERAMENT. Stolid is also distinct from this unit's Blase (unconcern from being jaded, not calm dependability) and Torpid (inactive, not emotionally steady).
